Cryptographic keys are only as good as the entropy behind them, yet most
embedded key generators are evaluated as black boxes: statistical test
suites are run on their output and a pass is taken as evidence of
randomness. This thesis first shows, on the hardware random number
generator of the ESP32, why that is not enough: its output passes NIST
SP~800-22 and scores like noise under the SP~800-90B estimators even
when, as a restart test reveals, it is a fixed pseudo-random sequence ---
and NIST itself has since rejected the first suite for assessing
cryptographic generators. It then takes the opposite route: a white-box
key-generation engine whose entropy
is justified from the physics of the device. A ring-oscillator entropy
source is designed at transistor level and its jitter is extracted from
simulation and turned, through a validated stochastic model, into a lower
bound on min-entropy per bit and into the design parameters of the
sampler. Around it, a fully portable digital core --- SP~800-90B health
tests, an AES-based conditioning and \acs{CTRDRBG} with derivation
function, AES-CMAC authentication and an \acs{I2C} register interface ---
is written once and verified three ways: against the official test
vectors, in simulation on a Basys~3 FPGA acting as the verification
vehicle, and against an ESP32 that recomputes every result with an
independent implementation (mbedtls). The same VHDL is finally
synthesized on an open 130~nm standard-cell library to give the area in
gate equivalents and the path to a dedicated integrated circuit. All
code, models, vectors and data are released.

Cryptographic keys are only as good as the entropy behind them, yet most
embedded key generators are evaluated as black boxes: statistical test
suites are run on their output and a pass is taken as evidence of
randomness. This thesis first shows, on the hardware random number
generator of the ESP32, why that is not enough. Its output passes NIST
SP~800-22, and on twenty-six captures in four operating conditions the
non-IID estimators of SP~800-90B credit it with 0.81 to 0.92 bit of
min-entropy per bit, with no resolvable difference between conditions or
between two chips; yet a restart test on one chip shows that, with the
radio and the ADC off, the output is a pseudo-random sequence seeded only
during boot, which the estimators credit as much as with the radio on.
NIST itself has since rejected SP~800-22 for assessing cryptographic
generators. The thesis then takes the opposite route: a ring-oscillator
\acs{TRNG} whose entropy is bounded from the physics of the device, as
the source of a key-generation engine intended for integration as an
application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC), with the ESP32 figures as
the reference against which the built source is to be compared under the
same methodology. The source is an elementary ring oscillator, a ring
sampled by a second one; the ring is designed at transistor level on
the open IHP SG13G2 130~nm process and simulated with injected noise
whose density is taken from its own device models. The jitter extracted
from the waveforms, 180~fs per period against a numerical floor of
0.70~fs, is turned, through a stochastic model checked against an exact
computation, into a lower bound on min-entropy per bit and into the
sampler divider that meets the AIS~20/31 target, at a few kbit/s per
ring. The engine around the source --- SP~800-90B health tests,
AES-based conditioning and \acs{CTRDRBG}, AES-CMAC authentication and an
\acs{I2C} register interface --- is written once in portable VHDL and
verified in simulation against the official test vectors and against an
independent reference model in Python. Synthesized on the same open
library, the unoptimized digital engine takes 68 thousand gate
equivalents of cells without its test capture buffer, a lower bound
before placement and routing; the cost and schedule of a dedicated
integrated circuit are stated, and no chip is fabricated. For the
hardware, the same RTL targets a Basys~3 FPGA board, where the rings are
built from LUTs, and a separate ESP32 board attached over \acs{I2C} is
to act as host and independent verifier, recomputing the engine's
authentication tags with mbedtls. The verifier firmware is built; the
board-level run, including the entropy campaign that places the
min-entropy of the built rings beside the ESP32 figure, is a fixed
protocol still pending. All code, models, vectors and data are
released.

\section{Conclusions}

This thesis set out to characterize the generator of the ESP32 as a black
box, to design a ring-oscillator \ac{TRNG} as the source of a
key-generation engine intended for an integrated circuit, and to compare
the randomness of both under one methodology. At the time of writing,
the characterization of the ESP32 and the design of the source and of
the engine are closed; the measurement of the source as built is not.

The ESP32 reference is measured \meas{}. On twenty-six captures from two
identified chips and one unidentified board, its non-IID min-entropy is
0.81 to 0.92 bit per bit, with no effect of the operating condition or
of the chip at the resolution of the estimators, and its IID figure sits
at the resolution ceiling of the estimator. The restart test, run on one
chip, shows what those figures cannot: with the radio and the ADC off,
the output is a deterministic sequence seeded during boot, which the
estimators credit with 0.85 bit per bit, as much as with the radio on;
with the boot noise removed, every restart reads a window on one fixed
sequence, worth 6.5 to 10.8 bits per restart, and the test fails; with
the Wi-Fi started, the generator does receive noise.

The ring has been designed at transistor level: five stages with their
enable gate, on the open IHP SG13G2 process, simulated with injected
noise whose density is taken from its own device models. The bench
declared its resolution first, 0.70~fs, 259 times below the 180~fs of
jitter per 366~ps period that the device noise produces \simu{}; the
jitter accumulates as white noise (exponent 1.05) and doubles when the
noise density is quadrupled. Three limits go with that figure: the noise
is injected as a stationary source, which may overestimate the thermal
variance by up to a factor of two or underestimate it by an amount not
yet quantified; only the typical corner at 27~$^\circ$C and 1.2~V has
been simulated; and at the operating divider flicker noise dominates the
accumulated variance, so the jitter that sets the entropy bound must be
measured at short accumulation.

Through the Wiener-phase model of Baudet
\emph{et al.}~\cite{baudet_2011_security}, evaluated exactly with the
wrapped Gaussian, that jitter becomes a quality factor per sampling
period. Two properties of the model were established rather than
assumed: the series usually cited as a lower bound overestimates the
entropy, and the first-harmonic min-entropy agrees with the exact one.
The min-entropy criterion of AIS~20/31 ($H_\infty \ge 0.98$,
$Q \ge 0.2286$) is met with a divider of $2^{20}$, at about 2.6~kbit/s
per ring, and the set point $Q = 0.30$ with $2^{21}$ \est{}. The bound
credits only the thermal component of the jitter. The comparison that
the title asks for is therefore asymmetric in kind before any number is
placed beside another: the ESP32 can be measured but not bounded, and
the designed source has a bound that a measurement must now confirm.

The engine around the source uses AES as its single primitive. Its
digital core is portable VHDL-2008; it passes its seven testbenches in
simulation, against the official vectors and against a bit-exact
reference model that reproduces the 960 \ac{CAVP} cases \simu{}. Without
the test capture buffer it synthesizes on the open IHP SG13G2 library to
68~kGE of cells \simu{}, a lower bound before placement and routing,
which three optimizations not yet synthesized would bring to about
38~kGE \est{}. No chip was fabricated, and the engine has not been
placed, routed or checked for timing on that process, nor simulated
together with its transistor-level ring; the cost and schedule of an
academic shuttle are stated instead.

What remains open is the hardware: the rings built on the \ac{FPGA}, the
entropy campaign run through the same SP~800-90B battery as the ESP32 at
the same sample size, and the board-level run with the ESP32 as
independent verifier. Until it is done, the min-entropy of the built
source is not bounded and no value is claimed for it.

\item \label{step:esp32cmp}\textbf{Compare with the ESP32 reference} of
Section~\ref{sec:esp32_90b} under the same analysis: the same tool and
version, both tracks, the bit layout, at least six captures of $10^6$
bits, and the one-way analysis of variance per estimator with the
correction for eleven tests already used between conditions and chips,
now with the source as the factor. The engine's raw bits arrive in chunks
of 4096 consecutive bits from the capture buffer, because the design has
no path that streams them out continuously; Section~3.1.1 of the
standard accepts the concatenation of chunks of at least 1000
consecutive samples only when $10^6$ consecutive samples cannot be
produced, which is the case for this design, and the difference from the
long consecutive streams of the ESP32 is stated with the result. Two
levels are compared and kept apart: the engine's raw bits against the
ESP32 output, where only the engine is assessed as the standard intends,
and the engine's \ac{DRBG} output against the ESP32 output, two outputs,
like with like; at that level the estimators can only show whether
either output is distinguishable from uniform, not what entropy lies
behind it. The model's bound, which the ESP32 cannot supply, is reported
beside the estimates and not merged with them.
\end{enumerate}

Until step 4 closes, the engine's claim is precise and limited: the chain
from physical noise to key material is designed, written in VHDL and
verified in simulation against the standards, and the bound it will
produce is computable from a measurement that has not yet been taken.

\label{sec:objectives}

The thesis has two parts. The first characterizes the generator of the
ESP32 as a black box (Section~\ref{sec:background}) and provides the
reference for the comparison. The general objective of the second is to
design a cryptographic key-generation engine intended for integration as
an \ac{ASIC}: an entropy source built from ring oscillators designed at
transistor level, and a digital core that turns its bits into keys and
uses them. The FPGA serves that objective as the verification vehicle
and as the hardware on which rings of the same architecture are built
from its own logic and measured; the ESP32, on a separate board, serves
both as an independent oracle for the digital core and as the reference
generator against which the random sequences are compared. The specific
objectives are the following.

\begin{enumerate}

The second part builds the generator instead of measuring someone
else's: an engine whose entropy source is designed, whose jitter is
measured inside the device, whose min-entropy follows from a model, and
whose keys are produced and used by primitives verified against the
standards. The ESP32 changes role from subject to judge. It has its own
AES and SHA accelerators and a mature cryptographic library, so it can
recompute everything the engine produces with an implementation that

from the inside: a ring-oscillator source whose circuit is designed,
whose jitter is measured inside the device, whose min-entropy follows

\chapter{Register Map}
\label{app:regs}

The engine is an \ac{I2C} slave at address \texttt{0x30} (7~bits). The
host writes a register address and then reads or writes data; the pointer
auto-increments on multi-byte accesses. The bus runs at up to 400~kHz and
the slave never stretches the clock: long commands are issued by writing
CONTROL and polled through the busy bit of STATUS. Names in parentheses

\toprule
Bit & Name & Meaning \\

3 & apt\_alarm & proportion test tripped (biased source) \\
4 & key\_valid & a key is loaded in the authenticator \\

\toprule
Bit & Command & Effect \\
\midrule
0 & seed & collect 384 raw bits (256 of entropy, 128 of nonce) and instantiate the DRBG from scratch \\
1 & generate & take 256 bits from the DRBG; the first 128 become the key, the rest are discarded, and the CMAC sub-keys are reloaded; outside test mode nothing of it is readable \\
2 & authenticate & TAG $\leftarrow$ CMAC$_{\mathrm{KEY}}$(CHALLENGE) \\

left to the host, which reads REQUESTS and issues \emph{reseed} far below
the $2^{48}$ limit of SP~800-90A. The key and the capture buffer are
readable only while the test pin is asserted.

cambios.texto_nuevo:
Following Baudet \emph{et al.}~\cite{baudet_2011_security}, the phase
$\varphi(t)$ of RO1, measured in periods, is modeled as a Wiener process
with drift $\mu$ and volatility $\sigma^2$. Only the thermal (white) part
of the jitter enters $\sigma^2$: its variance grows linearly with time
and its increments are independent, which is what a Wiener process
assumes. Flicker noise makes the variance grow faster than linearly, and
global jitter from the supply and substrate can be known or induced by
an adversary (Section~\ref{sec:soa_models}); neither is credited: both
are treated as known, so they add phase variance but no entropy. RO2 is
taken as a jitter-free time base: its own jitter would add to $Q$ only
if it were independent of that of RO1, which only a measurement on
hardware can show.

With $\sigma/T$ measured per period, $Q_{\mathrm{raw}} = (\sigma/T)^2$ and
the divider follows from $K_D = \lceil Q_{\mathrm{target}} /
Q_{\mathrm{raw}} \rceil$. For the range of jitter expected in a 28~nm
process the divider lies between $3\times10^4$ and $5\times10^5$ and the
throughput per ring between 1 and 20~kbit/s. The model reproduces the
published design point of Fischer and Lubicz ($K_D \approx 430\,000$ for
$\sigma = 5.01$~ps over $T = 7.81$~ns)~\cite{fischer_2014_embedded}. Such
rates are sufficient here: seeding the deterministic generator with
256~bits of full entropy requires about 512 raw bits at $H_\infty \approx
0.98$, i.e.\ between 0.03 and 0.5~s per seed, and the engine issues a seed
only at start-up and at reseed intervals.
cambios.texto_nuevo:
With $\sigma$ measured per period $T_1$ of RO1 and RO2 of period $T_2$,
the phase variance accumulated per period of RO2 is
$Q_{\mathrm{raw}} = (T_2/T_1)(\sigma/T_1)^2$, which reduces to
$(\sigma/T)^2$ for two identical rings. Then $Q = K_D\,Q_{\mathrm{raw}}$:
the required divider is $\lceil Q_{\mathrm{target}} / Q_{\mathrm{raw}}
\rceil$, and the one programmed is the smallest power of two not below
it, since the sampler implements only powers of two;
Section~\ref{sec:ihp_ring} applies this to the simulated ring. For the
range of jitter expected in a 28~nm process, with RO2 at 500~MHz, the
required divider lies between $3\times10^4$ and $5\times10^5$ and the
throughput per ring between 1 and 20~kbit/s. The transistor-level ring
on the 130~nm IHP SG13G2 process has less relative jitter per period,
$\sigma/T = 4.93\times10^{-4}$ \simu{}, and needs a larger divider,
$2^{20}$ \est{}; but an identical sampling ring runs at 2.73~GHz rather
than 500~MHz, so its throughput, 2.6~kbit/s \est{}, still falls inside
that range. The model reproduces the published design point of Fischer
and Lubicz: with their $\sigma = 5.01$~ps, $T_1 = 8.9$~ns,
$T_2 = 8.7$~ns and their target of 0.997~bit of Shannon entropy through
\eqref{eq:baudet14}, it gives $K_D = 431\,153$ against their
$\approx 430\,000$~\cite{fischer_2014_embedded}. Such rates are
sufficient here: each seed takes 384 raw bits, 256 of entropy input and
128 of nonce (Section~\ref{sec:drbg}), i.e.\ between 0.02 and 0.4~s per
seed; at $H_\infty \ge 0.98$ the entropy input carries about 250 bits of
min-entropy, and the engine issues a seed only at start-up and at reseed
intervals.

probability of any output vector, and an expression usually cited as a
lower bound on the Shannon entropy rate,
$H \ge 1 - \frac{4}{\pi^2\ln 2}e^{-4\pi^2 Q}$;
Chapter~\ref{ch:ch3_entropy} shows that its right-hand side is an
asymptotic expansion that overestimates the entropy, not a bound. In
design quantities, for RO1 of period $T_1$ sampled every $K$ periods
$T_2$ of RO2, with thermal jitter $\sigma_{th}$ per period,
$Q = K\,(T_2/T_1)\,(\sigma_{th}/T_1)^2$, and Fischer and Lubicz invert
the expression to obtain the divider $K_D$ from a measured
jitter~\cite{fischer_2014_embedded}. Petura \emph{et al.} print the
rewritten form as $H = 1 - \frac{4}{\pi^2\ln2}\exp(-\pi^2\sigma_{th}^2 K
T_2/T_1^3)$~\cite{petura_2016_survey}; read with $\sigma_{th}$ as the
jitter per period, as here, its exponent is $\pi^2 Q$ instead of
$4\pi^2 Q$, a factor of four in the divider. This work uses the form of
Fischer and Lubicz, which reproduces their published design point
(Section~\ref{sec:kd}).

\section{Contributions}

Each contribution is stated in the guarded form of
Section~\ref{sec:gap}: not found in the literature consulted, not claimed
as absent from it.

\begin{enumerate}
\item A ring oscillator for an entropy source, designed at transistor
level on an open \ac{PDK}, with the density of the injected noise taken
from the device models, the numerical floor of the bench declared before
any figure, and the thermal and flicker components separated by the
bench and by the impulse sensitivity function.
\item The chain \emph{jitter $\to$ quality factor $\to$ min-entropy bound
$\to$ divider $\to$ health-test cutoffs} applied to that ring against
AIS~20/31 version~3.0, with the exact wrapped-Gaussian computation in
place of the truncated series of Baudet \emph{et al.}, which was shown to
overestimate entropy.
\item An SP~800-90B characterization of the ESP32 generator on two
identified chips and an earlier, unidentified board, in four operating
conditions, with the IID tests calibrated at the sample size used, and a
restart test on one chip showing that, with the radio and the ADC off,
its output is pseudo-random and seeded only by the noise of the
bootloader.
\item A key-generation engine built around the source with AES as its
single primitive, written as portable \ac{RTL}, verified against official
vectors and synthesized on an open 130~nm library, with the area stated
as a lower bound.
\end{enumerate}
